headline: High: gpt-engineer can write and run code in a shared project directory, while awesome-prompts is a prompt source with no isolation, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a content-writing prompt repository, so its outputs can be copied into gpt-engineer prompts. gpt-engineer writes files and offers to run generated code, and its project-directory sharing plus no default isolation makes prompt content a plausible control channel. This is not proven direct ingestion, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF outputs from awesome-prompts are pasted into gpt-engineer prompts or files
IF gpt-engineer treats project files as trusted instructions
mitigations: Keep prompt libraries separate from the project directory
Add a manual review step before copying prompts into gpt-engineer
Use a read-only prompt source folder
Disable execution of generated code until prompts are sanitized

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts touches no data classes and has no network egress, while gpt-engineer reads and writes the user project directory and can call external model APIs. The pair does not show a shared sensitive-data channel by default, but if prompt content or project files contain secrets, gpt-engineer can transmit them outward. The blast radius is limited to the project workspace.
conditions: IF secrets are stored in the project directory used by gpt-engineer
IF copied prompt content includes confidential material
mitigations: Remove secrets from the project directory before use
Store prompts in a separate non-sensitive workspace
Redact confidential text before pasting into gpt-engineer
Restrict outbound model access to approved endpoints

C_capability_conflict.rationale: gpt-engineer supports per-project shared state via the project directory and can write files, while awesome-prompts is a source of prompt content that may also be edited or mirrored into that same directory. Even though awesome-prompts itself is not runnable, the pair can still contend over the same mutable workspace if co-located. Uncertainty about actual co-location pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF prompt files and generated code are edited concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate directories for prompts and code
Use a lock file during edits
Run only one writer at a time
Snapshot the workspace before generation

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts can supply instructions that gpt-engineer may treat as authoritative prompt material, and gpt-engineer then writes code based on that input. Because gpt-engineer can execute generated code with the user's privileges, a bad prompt can cascade into incorrect or harmful code generation. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF awesome-prompts content is used as an input prompt for gpt-engineer
IF generated code is executed without independent review
mitigations: Require human review of generated code before execution
Use a test-only project for first runs
Limit execution privileges in the shell environment
Compare generated files against the intended spec

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or retention obligations are documented for awesome-prompts, while gpt-engineer handles generated source code and OpenAI API keys. The pair therefore has only a generic compliance surface, not a documented residency mismatch. Because the evidence is sparse, I keep this low and do not cite a second agent-specific compliance claim beyond the documented surfaces.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the gpt-engineer project directory
IF the configured model backend stores prompts outside the required jurisdiction
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in the workspace
Confirm backend data-processing terms before use
Separate secret material from generated code
Document retention expectations for the project
